“Indicators of economic activity and employment have continued to strengthen” signals a tight labor market and unemployment likely below or near its natural rate, which, in Taylor rule–type prescriptions, warrants higher policy rates. The Committee’s 25 bp hike, signaling of “ongoing increases,” and plans to reduce balance sheet holdings align with modern implementation frameworks (Goodfriend 2002 on interest on reserves and operating targets) and with inflation-forecast–based strategies aimed at anchoring expectations (Svensson and Woodford 2005). While the statement is bolstered by strong job gains, it emphasizes elevated inflation from pandemic-driven supply/demand imbalances and energy shocks intensified by the Russia–Ukraine war—consistent with literature on cost-push pressures and a steeper, less favorable Phillips curve trade-off in the short run (“The Bones and Shapes of the Phillips Curve,” and COVID-era measurement issues like shifting consumption baskets noted in “COVID-19 Inflation Weighting in Israel”). The dissent favoring a 50 bp move reflects the case for front-loading when the inflation-at-risk distribution has fat upper tails (“Mixing it up: Inflation at risk”), though the price-puzzle literature cautions that measured inflation may not fall immediately after hikes. Net tone: cautiously hawkish—positive on labor, guarded on growth, focused on restoring price stability.
